prompt.context: Milk & Cheese, Inc. (MCI) is a leading producer of dairy, ham and sausages in the US. Currently it produces more than 1,000 products. MCI and two competitors dominate this market. MCI wants to increase its profits and has hired your firm to help. Another team in your firm is already working on costs and expenses; your team is focusing on MCI's product portfolio.
prompt.question: Your role is to analyze which, if any, of the company's 1,000+ products MCI should stop producing/selling. How would you do that?

clarifying_info.q: Is MCI interested in acquiring a competitor or expanding overseas?
clarifying_info.a: No, MCI is not interested in either of those options.

clarifying_info.q: What data is available for the product portfolio?
clarifying_info.a: You can get a product listing with margin and volume data for each product.

clarifying_info.q: What are MCI's target or acceptable margin levels?
clarifying_info.a: Average margin is 16%; average volume is 35K tons. Assume no relevant difference in prices among products.

clarifying_info.q: Does SG&A change if we alter the product mix?
clarifying_info.a: No, SG&A is not affected by potential changes in product mix.

exhibits.title: Scatter Plot: Margin vs. Volume by Product
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot with margin on one axis and volume on the other, displaying the position of MCI's 1,000+ products relative to the average margin (16%) and average volume (35K tons). Products are grouped into four quadrants labeled A, B, C, and D.
exhibits.data: Average margin = 16%; Average volume = 35K tons; quadrants A (high margin, high volume), B (high margin, low volume), C (low margin, high volume), D (low margin, low volume)

exhibits.title: Pareto (80/20) Chart: Products vs. Cumulative Profit
exhibits.shows: A Pareto chart showing cumulative profit contribution as a percentage against the number of products ranked from highest to lowest contribution. The chart is divided into two categories: Category I (the ~80% of profit coming from ~800 products) and Category II (the remaining ~20% of profit coming from the bottom ~200 products).
exhibits.data: Category I: ~800 products contributing ~80% of cumulative profit; Category II: ~200 products contributing ~20% of cumulative profit

framework: Revenue analysis: understand revenue streams by product — price, volume, and revenue contribution
Cost analysis (COGS): understand cost per unit and total COGS by product to compute gross margin
SG&A allocation: note that SG&A is fixed and not affected by product mix changes
Portfolio segmentation: use a margin vs. volume scatter plot (or Pareto/80-20 analysis) to identify low-contribution products
Decision on problematic products: evaluate options — discontinue, sell to competitors, or investigate growth potential
Risk assessment: analyze risks of each option (e.g., selling to a major competitor may strengthen a rival)

questions.prompt: How would you structure the analysis to identify which products MCI should stop producing or selling?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates immediately recognize this is a profitability/portfolio rationalization problem. They should propose analyzing a product-level data set (revenue/COGS, or margin and volume). They should converge on a scatter plot (margin vs. volume) or Pareto chart as the best visualization for 1,000+ products. Key insight: frame it as 'find the products with low margin AND low volume — they add little profit and consume resources.'

questions.prompt: Using the scatter plot (Exhibit 1), which products should MCI target for removal?
questions.guidance: The candidate should divide the scatter plot into four quadrants using the averages (margin = 16%, volume = 35K tons) as axes. Quadrant D (low margin, low volume) contains the target products. Assuming at least 200 products are in each zone, there are approximately 200 products in quadrant D that contribute minimally to profit.

math.setup: Averages used as quadrant dividers: margin = 16%, volume = 35K tons. Quadrants: A = high margin & high volume (keep, star products); B = high margin & low volume (keep or investigate scale-up); C = low margin & high volume (investigate — volume may justify cost reduction); D = low margin & low volume (target for discontinuation).
steps: Identify products below average margin (16%) AND below average volume (35K tons) → Quadrant D
Assume at least 200 products fall in Quadrant D (roughly 20% of 1,000+ products)
math.answer: ~200 products in Quadrant D are primary candidates for removal from the portfolio

questions.prompt: Using the Pareto chart (Exhibit 2), how many products account for 80% of MCI's profit?
questions.guidance: The Pareto/80-20 rule shows that Category I (~800 products) drives ~80% of cumulative profit, while Category II (~200 products) contributes only ~20%. The ~200 products in Category II are the 'problematic' products.

steps: Category I: 80% of products (≈800) → 80% of cumulative profit
Category II: 20% of products (≈200) → 20% of cumulative profit
math.answer: ~200 products (Category II) contribute only ~20% of profit and are candidates for portfolio removal

questions.prompt: What options does MCI have for dealing with the ~200 problematic products, and what are the risks?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates propose multiple options beyond simply stopping production: (1) discontinue production outright, (2) sell/license products to minor competitors, (3) invest to improve margin or volume if growth potential exists, (4) bundle with high-margin products. Risks to discuss: selling to a major competitor could strengthen a rival; discontinuing products may alienate some customer segments; supply-chain or contract implications.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the options MCI should consider when dealing with the ~200 low-margin, low-volume products?

categories.name: Discontinue
ideas: Stop production of products with no strategic value
Avoid sunk-cost bias; assess exit costs (inventory, contracts)
Free up manufacturing capacity for high-margin products

categories.name: Sell or Divest
ideas: Sell product lines to smaller/regional competitors
License brand or recipe to third parties
Avoid selling to major competitors that could gain market share

categories.name: Improve or Reposition
ideas: Investigate whether volume can be grown (marketing, distribution)
Explore cost reduction to improve margin (supplier renegotiation, automation)
Bundle low-margin products with premium products to drive mix

categories.name: Analyze Growth Potential
ideas: Check if any low-margin products are in fast-growing categories
Assess whether margin is structurally low or a temporary issue
Consider consumer trends — e.g., health-focused dairy products

recommendation: Based on the portfolio analysis, approximately 200 products (those in Quadrant D of the scatter plot / Category II of the Pareto chart) are not contributing meaningfully to MCI's profit — they exhibit both below-average margin (< 16%) and below-average volume (< 35K tons).
MCI should consider removing these products from its portfolio, either by discontinuing production or by selling them to minor competitors.
risks: Selling problematic products to major competitors could strengthen rivals and jeopardize MCI's competitive position — prefer divestiture to smaller or regional players.
Discontinuing products may upset some customers or disrupt distribution agreements; a phased wind-down is advisable.
A small subset of low-margin, low-volume products may have strategic importance (e.g., anchor items for key retail accounts) and should be evaluated individually before removal.
next_steps: Conduct detailed analysis of each of the ~200 candidate products to confirm no strategic exceptions.
Identify potential buyers (minor competitors, regional brands) for products to be divested.
Model the profit uplift from freeing manufacturing capacity and reallocating to high-margin products.
Engage sales and operations teams to plan a phased product wind-down with minimal customer disruption.
